title: Knock and greet
hookLine: don't enter houses until you've asked permission and greeted the people (24:27)
tomorrow: Don't you want to be forgiven?

cards: Commentators on this verse describe an older habit. A visitor would walk straight into a house and call out a greeting once already inside, good morning, to someone who might not be ready to be seen.

Sometimes a curtain was all that stood in the way. Surah An-Nur, a surah full of rules about privacy and dignity, sets down a small one about thresholds. It's so ordinary you could miss how much it says.

teach.h: ENTER NOT HOUSES NOT YOUR OWN.
teach.b: Verse twenty-seven. Pickthall begins: "O ye who believe! Enter not houses other than your own".
Not until you've made yourselves known, and greeted the people inside with peace. The verb for making yourself known is tasta'nisu.

Commentators link it to uns, the word for ease, friendliness, feeling at home with someone. So it isn't only asking permission. It's waiting until the people inside are comfortable with you being there.
The next verse adds: if you find no one at home, don't go in. And if you're told to go back, go back; that is purer for you. No argument, no peering through the window.
The hadith fill in the picture. Bukhari records Abu Musa going to 'Umar's house, asking permission three times, getting no answer, and leaving.

teach.h: ASK THREE TIMES, THEN GO BACK.
teach.b: When 'Umar later asked why he'd left, Abu Musa said the Prophet ﷺ taught: ask permission three times, and if you're not given it, go back.

teach.h: STAND TO ONE SIDE OF THE DOOR.
teach.b: Another report, in Abu Dawud, says that when the Prophet came to someone's door, he would stand to one side of it, not facing straight in, and give the greeting.

That's the whole lesson in a posture: stand where you can't see in, say peace, wait. So knock and greet isn't fussy etiquette. It's respect for another person's space, the part of their life they get to decide about.
Today doors have locks and houses have bells, but the same idea reaches a bedroom door, a phone left on a table, a message thread that isn't yours.

how: Muslim families often teach children to knock, say as-salamu 'alaykum and wait before entering a room, following 24:27–28 and the hadith on asking permission three times.

o: the right to enter a relative's home
ease, the welcome a visitor waits for
the greeting of peace said at a door

games.q: at the threshold — tap the pairs.
p: make yourself known, until they're at ease
ask, then go back if unanswered
where the Prophet stood at a door

s: the verse says if no one is home, you may go in
24:28 says if no one is there, don't enter.
commentators link tasta'nisu to a word for ease and friendliness
it means waiting until the people inside are comfortable with you.
Abu Musa kept knocking until 'Umar answered
he asked three times, got no answer, and left, as the Prophet taught.

games.q: you've come to a friend's house. you've called out a greeting three times. no answer. what do you do?
o: look through the window to check.
games.why: go back. Abu Musa did exactly this at 'Umar's house, citing the Prophet: ask three times, then return.

practice: Think of the doors you go through without knocking: a family member's room, a colleague's desk, a friend's phone, a shared screen.

Picture yourself standing beside one of them, knocking, and waiting a few breaths longer than feels natural, until you're welcome. If you pray, you can say the greeting of peace to yourself as you picture it.

wordCard.voice: Uns. Ease, the familiarity a visitor waits for before entering: make yourself known, say peace, and wait until you're welcome. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: make yourselves known, until there is ease; from uns, familiarity. 24:27.

carryVoice: Your line: ask before entering. Peace first, then wait to be welcome. Four hundred ninety-five days in.
